chapter: Technique, New Orleans influence and the school's future
title: Holding the horn and fingering in New Orleans playing
summary: DeVore says New Orleans players aim the horn up and out, mentioning Percy Humphrey's fingering and Eddie Pearson.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Cornet or trumpet: choosing and owning horns

blocks.x: Do you think there's anything distinctive about the mechanics of New Orleans playing? How you hold your hands or how you finger?

Well, from my own observation, not particularly. I watch Percy's playing. He fingers his instrument extremely legitimate. Fingers all the way at the tips of his fingers. When he holds his horn and he's using his instrument, he does. But when he's playing and he's holding his horn with his left hand, he's not using the ring, you know. And the classical men don't like rings on horns. Because they say it interferes with the... When you play, see those two fingers go together like that. And that would interfere with the motion. If you held that solid, it would interfere with the motion of your fourth finger there. So I've seen both of them. I've seen some players come all the way over. I don't think there's any particular... I'll tell you one thing distinctive though. Hold your horn up and even a little bit high. All of them do that. You never see a New Orleans musician point his horn to the ground and play down on the ground. That I can recall. Maybe there were some, but I just can't recall them right now. They all play with their horns straight out, aiming that tone out there so it's bouncing off a wall 40 feet away. Or going out in the thin air if you're playing a parade. The guys that didn't do that were the guys that didn't sound so good. Like this... I remember that's what Eddie Pearson said. Eddie Pearson always pointed his horn way out. And the other guy used to play with Eddie Pearson. He played with Paul Barber. He's a big, heavy set guy with a... He was a lot of sliding and stuff. Kind of a brassy, not really a real jazzy trombone player. Turbulon, I guess that was his name. Clemon. Yeah, he'd aim his horn down. Like... Yeah. With kind of bad hair, you know. But that's about the only thing I can say about holding the instruments. Aiming the horns up. Helps your playing. I mean that way I think you can get your singing. I think you can get the singing, aiming your horn down on the floor. Get the singing quality of it.
